title: Devanagari
hook: a curl that stands in front of the letter it follows
tomorrow: if every letter carries an a, how does a word end without one?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Devanagari's head line: one bar holds one word, and where it breaks, a new one starts. Today, a vowel that cuts in line.

Midnight, a kitchen table, a birthday card with nothing in it yet. Someone is copying one word from a printed Gita: adhikara, the right, from the line you have the right to act, not to the fruit. A, fine. Then dha, and there's a curl standing in front of the dha, leaning over it like an umbrella. The word is said adhi. But the page seems to put the i first. The pen hovers. Is the book printed wrong, or is the eye?
screen: `A BLANK BIRTHDAY CARD.` → `ADHIKARA: THE RIGHT.` → `A CURL IN FRONT OF THE DHA.` → `PRINTED WRONG?`

segments.voice: Neither. That curl is the short i, and in Devanagari it's drawn before the consonant it follows in speech. Written first, said second. Every vowel except the built-in a gets a sign, a matra, attached to its consonant, and the short i's sign stands on the left, rising up and hooking over the letter, like an arm around a friend's shoulders. Now the part that makes it click. Its partner, the long i, written with a hook on the other side, comes after. Short i in front, long i behind. So ki and kee, side by side, look like mirror images. Why would a script do this? Because a Devanagari reader isn't reading letter, then vowel. The eye takes in the syllable, consonant and sign together, as one shape, and says it all at once. Dhi, not d, h, i. The curl isn't out of order; it's part of one picture. The same thing happens in the name Shiva: the i's curl leans over sha before you ever reach va. So the copier at the kitchen table does the brave thing. Draws the curl first, then the dha tucked under it, and says adhi. The card has its first syllable.
screen: `THE SHORT I: DRAWN FIRST, SAID SECOND.` · `A MATRA: THE VOWEL'S SIGN.` · `THE LONG I GOES BEHIND.` · `ONE LOOK, ONE SYLLABLE.` · then, large: `THE CURL IS PART OF THE PICTURE.`

segments.voice: With one fingertip, write on your open palm: first the curl, a tall stroke bending over to the right, then the letter underneath it, slowly enough to feel each stroke land. Only when both are drawn, say dhi, softly, on the out-breath. Draw it again with each breath, hand first, voice after.
Devanagari: a script built in syllables, where the short i's sign is drawn before the letter it follows.
For the road: Devanagari, where the curl goes first, the voice second, and the eye reads both as one. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Learners usually practice the vowel signs on each consonant in turn, ka, kaa, ki, kee and so on, writing and saying them together until each syllable is read at a glance.

fork.setup: your little cousin writes ki as the k and then the i sign after it, the way English would. what's the gentle fix?
options: the short i's curl goes in front, leaning over the k; you still say k first.
write the i as a separate letter after the k, like English.
leave it; the order of the signs doesn't change anything.
fork.reveal: the short i is drawn before its consonant and said after it. after the k is where the long i goes, so her version reads kee.

original.note: Sanskrit: the syllable dhi, from adhikara. The i's sign is drawn first, the dha under it.

what it means: it's the short i's sign, drawn before the consonant and said after it.
what a scholar hears: a script that writes syllables, consonant plus matra read as one unit; the short i in front, the long i behind.

chat.says: dad says Nani's fave line is the 'right to act' one. why is there an i BEFORE the dha??
options: it's the short i's sign. it's drawn first, but you say dha first: dhi.
it's a typo. in good editions the i always comes after the dha.
it means you say the i first, so the word is said aidha-kara.
chat.meaning: In Devanagari the short i's sign is drawn before its consonant and said after it, so धि reads dhi.

adhikara.meaning: a right; the word in the Gita's line about action

matra.meaning: a vowel's sign, attached to a consonant

Gita.meaning: the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna's teaching to Arjuna

Shiva.meaning: a great god of the Hindu tradition

notes: Answers 1428's question (why is one vowel written before the letter it's sounded after). Avoids 1427-1428's angles (akshara, the head line) except as review.
Script facts: the short i matra (ि) is written to the left of its consonant and pronounced after it; the long i matra (ी) is written to the right. Standard; confirm phrasing.
Gita 2.47 is paraphrased ('you have the right to act, not to the fruit'), as in camp 1. Adhikara glossed as 'the right'.
